carnage.name: IUDoc92
carnage.commentary: That’s a bogey with extra sauce: a par-4 turned into a seven, and the net math still only softened it so much. The round was mostly salvage mode, but this hole was the spreadsheet slamming its own face into the desk.

carnage.name: MattF
carnage.commentary: Opening with a six is a rude little thesis statement. The rest of the card never fully shook it off, which is how you end up fighting the round instead of playing golf.

carnage.name: MashedBROtato
carnage.commentary: A par-5 seven is ugly, but the real crime is letting a scoring hole become a momentum tax. That was the round’s sloppiest leak in an otherwise winner-level card.

carnage.name: Dan94
carnage.commentary: This was the kind of par-3 that sneaks in a stupid number and tries to pretend it’s fine. It wasn’t disastrous, just the one blemish that kept the card from looking absolutely filthy.

carnage.name: KeithK75
carnage.commentary: One extra shot on a par-5 doesn’t sound dramatic until you realize it was the only real opening for the course to bite back. The rest of the card was clean enough to make that one look annoyingly out of place.

carnage.name: BigTime
carnage.commentary: A par-3 bogey is the kind of hole that barely looks rude until you remember how tight this card was. That was the lone loose screw in a round where the irons otherwise did most of the heavy lifting.

players.name: MashedBROtato
players.tagline: The putter bailed out the crime scene just enough to collect the trophy.
players.body: He wins the net event by two over BigTime, and the gross card was good enough to keep the whole thing from looking like a fluke. This was a classic MashedBROtato round: the driver showed up loud, the putter did the emergency response work, and the ugly holes never quite got to write the final script. The power numbers were there, the short game was steady, and the flatstick poured in enough to cover for the fact that the tee game still left some fairways on the table. More importantly, this is the strong-trend version of him: not a random spike, but another start where he looked like the same guy who’s been living around the top of these boards all rolling history.

players.name: BigTime
players.tagline: When the approach play is this hot, the tee box can be a suggestion.
players.body: He finishes second in net and third in gross, and the card says the irons were doing the heavy lifting while the driver wandered off to find itself. BigTime’s approach play was the loud part of the round, backed by a clean fairway count and enough birdie chances to keep pressure on the front. The one blemish that matters is the par-3 bogey at 12, because on a card this sharp that’s the kind of hole that refuses to leave quietly. With a strong trend across five starts, this is less “hot streak” and more “yeah, this guy keeps showing up near the top because the iron game keeps cashing checks.”

players.name: Dan94
players.tagline: The irons were nasty; the card only got weird in one tiny corner.
players.body: He takes the gross win and still ends up third in net, which tells you exactly what kind of round this was: the raw golf was the best in the field, but net competition made him pay for the tiny wobble. Dan94 was striping it from tee to green, piling up birdie chances, and making enough putts to keep the whole thing moving fast. The only real blemish was the par-3 at 14, and even that was more nuisance than collapse. With a strong long-run profile and repeated top-tier gross finishes, this is basically the same dangerous version of Dan94 again: better raw golf than most of the room, and just enough net resistance to keep the trophy math interesting.

players.name: IUDoc92
players.tagline: The round had range, but the putter still filed an appeal against the rest of the bag.
players.body: He grabs fourth in net while the gross score tells the uglier truth: the ball-striking was functional, the scoring was not. IUDoc92 actually gave himself enough looks to make this respectable, but the putter and the 3-putt count kept turning decent holes into unnecessary paperwork. The double-bogey-style damage on 13 was the loudest leak, and the rest of the round never fully escaped that drag. Still, this is a better shape than his older profile, and the recent starts suggest he’s no longer just donating strokes to the course; he’s at least making the place work for them.

players.name: KeithK75
players.tagline: That’s a tidy round with one little par-5 tax bill attached.
players.body: He ends up fifth in net and second in gross, which is a pretty good summary of the day: the raw scoring was sharp, but the net leaderboard is where the actual damage got sorted out. KeithK75 gave the field a strong tee-to-green showing, hit a pile of greens, and kept the putter from turning into a full-blown hostage situation. The lone bogey on 11 is the only real blemish worth bothering with because everything else was basically a clean, efficient card. Across his recent starts, this is the reliable version of KeithK75: not flashy, just consistently good enough to hang around the top when the rest of the room starts spraying it.

players.name: MattF
players.tagline: Started with a faceplant and spent the rest of the day pretending it was fine.
players.body: He finishes last in net, and the opening six is doing a lot of the explaining. MattF still had enough tee and putting to avoid a total crater, but the round never fully escaped that early mess, and the rest of the card mostly looked like damage control instead of momentum. The weird part is that the ball-striking numbers weren’t disastrous; the misses just showed up in inconvenient places and kept the score from settling down. Given the stronger recent history, this reads more like a noisy outlier than a full identity crisis, but it was still the kind of round that makes the leaderboard laugh at you first and ask questions later.
